seo.title: Karmic tail 9 15 6 compatibility: silence, a bond, a free choice
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 15 6 compatibility: the couple starts in shared quiet, passes through an unspoken bargain and has to learn to choose each other freely.

title: Karmic tail 9-15-6 in compatibility: silence, a bond and a free choice
short: The Hermit, The Devil and The Lovers look like cards from three different stories: a quiet one, a dark one and a bright one. Yet the two outer numbers of this tail add up to the middle with nothing left over: 9 + 6 = 15. Silence plus desire makes a bond. That is the whole plot of the 9-15-6 tail in a compatibility matrix: the couple begins in careful quiet, on the way binds itself, almost without noticing, with a bargain nobody ever said out loud, and its main task is to choose each other again, of their own free will and in broad daylight.

sections.h2: The play this couple lives in
paragraphs: In 1888 Henrik Ibsen wrote The Lady from the Sea. It is staged less often than A Doll's House, although it reads easily as an answer to it: Nora left and slammed the door, while Ellida Wangel stays — but only after she has been given leave to go. The story of this marriage passes through three states, exactly in the order of our tail. Quotations from the play follow Eleanor Marx-Aveling's translation of 1890; where the Norwegian word matters, it is given.

A small fjord town in northern Norway. Wangel, the town's medical man and a widower with two daughters, married again five or six years ago — Ellida, the lighthouse keeper's daughter. The townspeople call her "the Lady from the Sea": she bathes in the fjord every day in any weather and says the water here is "sick". Ten years earlier, before the marriage, a sailor from an American ship, a man with a dark story, put his own ring and her small ring on a key-ring and threw them into the sea: now, he said, they were wedded to the sea. In the summer when the play begins, this Stranger comes back for her.
The three cards of the tail are three states of this marriage:

ul: **The Hermit:** a house where everyone has a corner and nobody asks anything;
**The Devil:** two agreements nobody truly chose — the vow to the sea and the marriage as a bargain;
**The Lovers:** in the last act the husband cancels the bargain, and the wife chooses him herself for the first time.

paragraphs: The plot looks like a love triangle, but that is not what Ibsen is writing about. In the final scene Wangel himself explains what the Stranger meant to his wife: "Your longing and aching for the sea, your attraction towards this strange man, these were the expression of an awakening and growing desire for freedom; nothing else." The same holds for the couple's tail: The Lovers do not stand for a third person. The "stranger" in a couple can be anything — a city they never lived in, a profession not chosen, an earlier life that still calls.

sections.h2: 9 · The Hermit at the entry: "if we happen to find there is anything to say"
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together and where it begins; the same point is its common language. With The Hermit this language is quiet. Both Wangels came to the marriage out of loneliness: he could no longer bear the emptiness of his house, and she, in her words, was "so helpless and bewildered, and so absolutely alone". Two people wanted a refuge — and got one.

Ibsen shows this house in the very first act. A guest asks where the lady of the house usually sits. She has her own arbour in the garden, the daughters sit on the verandah, and the husband goes to and fro — now to her, now to his children. "I think all parties feel most comfortable in this way," says Ellida. "You know we can talk across to one another — if we happen to find there is anything to say."

This is not coldness. The Hermit has a bright side, and in the play it is real: care. In all these years Wangel has never once asked who her former fiancé was. "You are always so thoughtful for me," Ellida tells him. Respect for boundaries, time and a place of one's own for solitude, an unhurried pace — that is this entry at its best. A couple that does not need to fill the silence with words is rare, and such couples treasure it.

But the entry stands on the line of the task, and the wish for quiet easily becomes resistance. In the Wangel house the silence has long since grown over everything. Every year the daughters secretly keep their late mother's birthday — with flowers and a flag — and claim it is all in honour of a guest; their father knows and says nothing. For three years Ellida has carried a fear her husband learns of only in the second act: "And you have gone about in this state three whole years, bearing for yourself this secret suffering, without confiding in me." The dread came back while she was expecting a child; the little boy died at a few months old, and since then she has not lived with her husband as his wife. That too they both leave unsaid.

Reviewing the old meanings of the cards, Waite recalls that Éliphas Lévi gave The Hermit to Prudence, and offers his own definition: "Prudence is the economy which follows the line of least resistance." Waite means a spiritual thrift, but in daily life the formula works literally. In the fourth act Ellida describes her marriage in just these terms: "I simply left things just as I found them the day I came here." Not one change, not one request, not one argument. Waite's reversed list for The Hermit even has a name for care taken to the limit: "unreasoned caution".

Wen tells two kinds of withdrawal apart. In the Four of Cups "the Seeker may be licking wounds"; in The Hermit the Seeker turns inward "in order to seek enlightenment". From outside they look the same. The Wangels' silence after their son's death seems to be a Four of Cups passing itself off as The Hermit. A couple with this tail does well to ask itself from time to time what it is holding — a lamp or a bandage.

In ordinary life it looks mundane. Two people love quiet evenings and do not pry into each other's souls. He does not ask why she is sad: "she'll tell me when she wants to." She does not say she feels hemmed in: "why worry him." There are no quarrels, because there are no conversations where a quarrel could happen. Among the minuses of The Hermit Lisovskaya names problems that pile up in silence. What goes unsaid does not disappear, and the middle of the tail shows what it turns into.

sections.h2: 15 · The Devil in the middle: a key-ring thrown into the sea
paragraphs: The middle of the task is what the couple goes through on the way from its shared wish to its main task. The Devil stands here, and in Ibsen it appears twice — as two agreements, neither of them truly chosen.

The first is the vow to the sea. The Stranger puts his ring and Ellida's small ring on a key-ring and throws it with all his might into the deep. "Had you no will of your own, then?" Wangel asks. "Not when he was near." Later she wrote to the sailor twice that it was all over, and he answered as if her letters did not exist: wait. This is The Devil without horns or hooves — a tie a person never chose and cannot leave by a single decision. Ellida finds a word for it sharper than any definition: "The terrible is that which repels and attracts."

The second agreement is the marriage itself. In the fourth act Ellida says what both have kept silent through all the years of marriage: "the truth — the pure and simple truth is — that you came out there and bought me." And at once: "Oh! I wasn't a bit better than you. I accepted the bargain. Sold myself to you!" Nobody lied and nobody played the villain: two lonely people made a sensible bargain. The Hermit plus The Lovers — and out came The Devil.

**The strangest thing in this middle is its language. The Devil here speaks in the words of freedom.** The Stranger once called himself Friman, which in Norwegian sounds almost like fri mand, "a free man"; in the fifth act he will say exactly that of himself: "I will live and die a free man." He does not claim Ellida by right: "If Ellida wishes to be with me she must come freely." And again: "Vows bind no one, neither man nor woman. If I hold so steadfastly to you, it is because I cannot do otherwise." A bond that calls itself freedom holds hardest of all: there is nothing to defend against. Yet without meaning to, it also points the way out. The word frivillig, "freely", is first spoken in the play by the Stranger, and Ellida at once repeats it twice to herself. The next day she will turn the word on her own marriage — "It was not freely that I went with you" — and tell her husband: "It all lies in those words. They have enlightened me."

Wangel answers the pull with a ban — and so he too ends up in the middle of the tail. "You have no choice, Ellida. You have no right to choose — no right without my permission." He threatens to have the Stranger arrested and plans to take his wife away to the sea air. And he names his own defeat: "So I have not won you by our living together. Never, never possessed you quite." Ellida answers with words anyone could say about control: "You can indeed keep me here! … But my mind — all my thoughts, all the longings and desires of my soul — these you cannot bind!"

Among the tasks of a couple with The Devil, Lisovskaya lists attempts to hold a partner through intimacy, a child, money or status, silence about one's own wishes, fear and hopelessness. In a 9-15-6 couple this middle grows out of the quiet of the entry. First "let's not talk about it", then unwritten clauses nobody signed: "I provide — you don't ask questions", "I put up with your silence — you don't leave", "we're together because it's too late to change anything", "he'd be lost without me". Each clause is reasonable on its own. Together they are a chain, and both of them hold it. Wen writes that The Devil "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame": a bond always contains more forces than one will. Ibsen has no villain, only two agreements everyone took part in.

To make the point plain, Ibsen sets a second couple beside the first. In the same last act Ellida's stepdaughter Bolette agrees to marry the no-longer-young Arnholm so that she can see the world: she cannot accept help from a friend, but she can accept a marriage. One bargain in the play is cancelled while another is struck before the audience's eyes.

The Devil has a bright side too, and Lisovskaya names it: speaking openly about desires and accepting each other's dark sides. The Wangels' first step out of the middle is the confession in the second act: Ellida tells him everything "just as it is", and her husband listens without passing sentence. Lisovskaya's chapter on The Devil ends with a short thought: nobody belongs to anybody. Ibsen reaches it three acts later.
If control in a relationship reaches threats or violence, it is no longer a matter for reading cards: real help is needed — an emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: 6 · The Lovers: cancel the bargain to make a union
paragraphs: The main task is the couple's chief trial, and it is read mostly through what does not work. With The Lovers it is choice. Not falling in love — the couple either had that at the start or did not — but the decision to be together, made freely and aloud. The difficulty is that such a choice is impossible while the bargain holds: from inside a cage one cannot choose the cage.

Ellida sees this before her husband does. She does not ask for a divorce — "I care nothing for such formalities" — but for both of them, "of our own free will", to release each other. And she explains: "I will not hide behind the fact that I am the wife of another man; nor make the excuse that I have no choice, for then it would be no decision."

Half an hour before the steamer's last bell, Wangel does what neither his wife nor the audience expects: "And so — so I cry off our bargain at once. Now you can choose your own path in perfect — perfect freedom." And he adds the essential thing: "for now you can choose in freedom, and on your own responsibility, Ellida." She repeats it as if tasting the words: **"In freedom, and on my own responsibility! Responsibility, too? That changes everything."**

She stays, and her explanation fits the whole tail: "I could have seen it — gone out into it, if only I myself had willed it. I could have chosen it. And that is why I could also renounce it." The Stranger leaves with the words: "There is something here stronger than my will." Nobody cut the bond — it lost its power the moment there was a choice.
Ibsen adds three last touches, and each answers a card of the tail.

ul: **To The Hermit:** "To think that now we can live wholly for one another —" Wangel begins, and Ellida finishes: "And with common memories. Yours, as well as mine." Two separate pasts become a common language.

**To The Devil:** Ellida calls her stepdaughters "ours" — "They who are not mine yet, but whom I shall win." The Norwegian here uses the same verb eje, "to own", as Wangel's "never possessed you". Owning has given way to winning.

**To The Lovers:** the younger daughter, seeing her father with her stepmother, whispers: "Why, she and father look exactly as if they were a betrothed couple!" After five or six years of marriage they are engaged for real for the first time.

paragraphs: Lisovskaya lists among the tasks of a couple with The Lovers what Ibsen lays out scene by scene. Learning to love oneself inside the couple — and Ellida voices the formula of this task: "Better the meanest work — better the poorest life — after one's own choice." The insecurity that breeds jealousy and control — Wangel, whose first words on learning about the Stranger are: "Only to think that all these three years you have cared for another man… Not for me — but for another!" Dependence on family — Ellida, who for years has lived amid another family's memories and says: "I haven't a key to give up." Idealisation — "I am not what you took me for." And the ability to get through a hard experience together — their son's death, which they could not talk about.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: a ring with two chains and the sun at its zenith
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own artwork, but Waite's description of his deck (1909) contains details that read like stage directions to The Lady from the Sea.

ul: **The Devil.** "There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female." One ring and two chains — the key-ring with two rings thrown into the sea. Ibsen wrote his scene twenty years before the deck, and the coincidence proves nothing, but it makes the mechanism visible: a single knot holds both.

**The Lovers.** "The sun shines in the zenith" — no shadow falls on the couple. Waite calls VI "the card of human love" and, in the same breath, "a mystery of the Covenant". In our reading this is the key to the main task: a covenant in the biblical sense is an agreement made openly and willingly. The Devil binds with a bargain, The Lovers with a covenant.

**The Moon** (the values of a third of these couples). "The path between the towers is the issue into the unknown", and what crawls out of the water "strives to attain manifestation… but as a rule it sinks back whence it came". Ellida takes leave of the Stranger in almost these words: "To me you are as one dead — who has come home from the sea, and who returns to it again."

**The Hanged Man and The World** (the couple's centre). Wen notes that the crossed legs of the hanged man reappear in the figure of The World and concludes that "it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card". For this tail the centre is always one of these two cards.

paragraphs: The 9-15-6 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 82 (1.217%) and ranks 28th among the 97 couple tails. Going through every date since 1900 shows things about it that three numbers alone do not.

**The middle adds itself up.** In a couple's matrix the middle is not derived from the outer numbers: each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Yet here 9 + 6 = 15 works out with no reduction, just as in a personal tail, where the middle is calculated exactly that way. That is why the order 9-15-6 also occurs for a single person — for 1,559 dates since 1900; that is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article on it. In a couple it helps to read the equation backwards: 15 − 9 = 6. Take the silence out of the bond and a choice remains. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

**Nobody brings their own Devil to the middle.** Numbers 13–22 in a couple's point come only from an exact sum, so the 15 in the middle is always the sum of two smaller personal middles. There are three recipes: 6 + 9 (43.9% of couples), 5 + 10 (28.2%) and 7 + 8 (27.9%). In our reading these are three ways of binding oneself: one partner's desire and the other's silence (The Lovers and The Hermit), a rule and circumstances (The Hierophant and The Wheel of Fortune), drive and a contract (The Chariot and Justice). The Wangels' marriage resembles the third recipe — a bargain honestly kept by both sides.

**The Devil is born between two people.** In no such couple do both partners have The Devil in their personal tails; in 44.3% of couples neither has it in the personal tail, and in 17.6% it is absent from all fifteen main points of both personal matrices. A tie that exists in neither person alone appears only in the couple — as in Ibsen, where there is no villain and yet there is a chain.

**The Devil may already be hiding in the entry.** In a third of couples (33%) the Hermit at the entry is made of personal entries 15 and 21 — one partner's Devil and the other's World: 15 + 21 = 36 → 9. The quiet a couple starts from sometimes already contains what it will turn into.

sections.h2: Centre and values: what holds the couple while it travels the tail
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the atmosphere between the two, what is not on show. With the 9-15-6 tail the centre comes in only two kinds.

**The Hanged Man — in 77.8% of couples.** Waite lists among its meanings wisdom, trials, sacrifice and intuition, and warns that in this card "all the significance is veiled". The atmosphere of such a couple is suspension: everything seems in place, but much is unnamed, and one partner carries the union for years. On the bright side Lisovskaya describes tact, attention and the ability to sense each other at a distance; on the dark side, the one who holds the relationship together with all their strength and receives reproaches in return. These are two sides of the same quiet. Wen calls the archetype of The Hanged Man "the wounded healer", and Wangel, a medical man who helps his wife at the cost of his own pain, fits the phrase literally. A centre of 12 is made of personal centres 4 + 8, 5 + 7 or 3 + 9.

**The World — in 22.2% of couples.** No individual ever has 21 at the centre: this atmosphere exists only in a couple. Almost always (in 21.2% of all such couples) it is made of personal centres 9 and 12 — one partner's Hermit and the other's Hanged Man. Waite's list for The World includes "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place" — everything the Stranger offers with his cabin on the steamer and everything Wangel offers when he plans to take his wife away to the sea. On the bright side The World's atmosphere is full acceptance and a shared philosophy of life; on the dark side, in Lisovskaya, many secrets and illusions about the relationship. The World inside a couple holds as long as it is not mistaken for escape.

**The couple's values — The Hermit (66.7%) or The Moon (33.3%).** Values are what the union exists for, and here the tail comes full circle. In two thirds of couples The Hermit appears twice: at the entry and in the values. What the couple began with as a hiding place has to become its chosen value: time of one's own, a place of one's own, a deep conversation — but as a home, not as a locked arbour. In a third of couples the value is The Moon. Wen recalls that tides are caused by the pull of the moon and writes that under this card "there is an external invisible force pulling on the Seeker", one the Seeker "must understand and work in harmony with". In the final scene Wangel tells his wife: "your mind is like the sea — it has ebb and flow." The value of such a couple is not the absence of a pull towards the unknown, but the ability to live with it together.
The partners' personal tails are 9-9-18 and 18-6-6. Neither of the two has The Devil at all — not in the tail, not at any other point of their personal matrices. It appears only in the sum.

The middle here is exactly the first recipe: The Hermit in the middle of one partner's personal tail and The Lovers in the middle of the other's. One partner's silence plus the other's desire. The couple's centre is The World (personal centres 9 and 12), the values are The Moon; this is the rarest pairing of centre and values for this tail, about 9% of couples.

The rest of the matrix repeats the tail. The Hermit also stands at "What to create together", "Home and things" and "Parents together" — four nines in all. The Lovers stand at "What fills", "Path to prosperity" and "What you teach" — four sixes. The Devil, absent from both partners, also stands at "Image of the couple": it is both the hidden middle of the road and what other people see; in Lisovskaya, The Devil in the image on its bright side is a vivid, passionate, unusual couple. Lisovskaya advises adding up repeats: four nines give 36 → 9, three Worlds (the centre, "Way into money", "What connects") give 63 → 9, two Moons ("Where it sparks" and the values) give 36 → 9. Everything comes back to The Hermit. In this couple the quiet sounds from every corner, and the tail shows what it can become.

sections.h2: How a couple lives 9-15-6 and what changes the script
paragraphs: The circle of this tail turns quietly. Two people carefully avoid the sore spot — that is the entry. What goes unsaid takes shape as unwritten terms, and each holds on to the union not because they choose it but because "that's how things are" — that is the middle. The way out is neither a break-up nor a new vow, but what Wangel did: lift the condition and ask again.

ul: **Say the bargain out loud.** Each unwritten clause — "I provide, you don't ask", "I put up with it, you don't leave" — should be talked through by both and decided anew: kept by free will or cancelled.

**Tell solitude from hiding.** Time and a place of one's own are The Hermit's bright side; a shared life where each sits in a separate arbour is its dark side. The test is simple: after the quiet, is there a wish to talk, or to hide further?
**Don't hold on by forbidding.** "I won't allow it" strengthens the pull; the question "are you staying?" weakens it. In Ibsen freedom is not a trick but a risk, and that is why it works.
**Choose the small things together.** Keys, money, a room, summer plans — decisions made by two, not inherited from an earlier life.
**Gather common memories.** "Yours, as well as mine": each one's past is not a hiding place but part of the common language.

paragraphs: The ending of the play is the strong version of the tail. In the first act the painter Ballested says he has settled in the town because he feels "united to the place by the bonds of time and habit". In the last he insists that people, unlike the mermaid, "can acclimatise themselves". Ellida corrects him: "In freedom they can, Mr. Ballested." Wangel adds: "And when they act on their own responsibility, dear Ellida." The same house, the same fjord, the same husband — but what holds them now is not habit but choice.

sections.h2: 9-15-6 and 9-6-15: the same cards in another order
paragraphs: The same numbers form one more couple tail — 9-6-15, the most common of all (4.627%, roughly every 22nd couple). There The Lovers are the middle of the road and The Devil is the main task: the couple travels through choice and learns not to turn love into a bond. With 9-15-6 it is the other way round: the bond is the road, and the choice is where the couple has to arrive.

ul: **9 · The Hermit — entry to the task.** This is where the couple starts and what it wants together: quiet, depth, a corner of its own where nothing needs explaining. It is also their common language — tact, hints, deeds instead of words. When the time comes to talk, the same quiet turns into resistance.

**15 · The Devil — middle of the task.** This is how the couple travels the road: through a bond. What goes unsaid thickens into unwritten terms — "that's how it turned out", "that's how it has to be", "where would we be without each other".
**6 · The Lovers — main task.** To cancel the bargain in order to make a union: to choose each other aloud, freely and on their own responsibility — and to learn to love themselves inside the couple.

intro: A couple's tail does not predict events or pass verdicts: it describes a task two people live through together. The evidence lies in the cards themselves, in the books about them and in the numbers.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 9-15-6 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's matrix: The Hermit at the entry to the task, The Devil in the middle, The Lovers as the main task. The couple starts from a shared wish for quiet and care, passes through unwritten agreements and attachment, and learns to choose each other freely and openly.

faq.q: Is the 9-15-6 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A tail does not predict events or grade a union; it describes a task. The Devil in the middle is not a verdict but a stretch of the road, and the way out is written into the same three cards: the free choice of The Lovers.

faq.q: How is the 9-15-6 tail calculated in a couple's matrix?
faq.a: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. For the dates 11.02.1976 and 04.07.1975: entry 9 + 18 = 27 → 9, middle 9 + 6 = 15, main task 18 + 6 = 24 → 6.

faq.q: How is the couple's 9-15-6 tail different from a personal 9-15-6 tail?
faq.a: The numbers are the same, but the calculation and the roles differ. A personal tail is calculated from one date and speaks about the person; a couple's tail is built from two matrices and describes the task of the union. A reading of one cannot be carried over to the other.

faq.q: How rare is the 9-15-6 tail among couples?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 82 (1.217%), 28th place among the 97 couple tails. The centre of such couples is The Hanged Man (77.8%) or The World (22.2%), the values are The Hermit (66.7%) or The Moon (33.3%).

report.h3: From inside a cage, nobody can choose the cage

report: The main task is The Lovers, and it is a choice. Not falling in love, but a decision to be together, made freely and aloud. While the bargain holds, no such decision exists. Ellida sees this first: "I will not … make the excuse that I have no choice, for then it would be no decision."

No holding on by forbidding: "I won't allow it" strengthens the pull, while the question "are you staying?" weakens it.
Make the small choices together — keys, money, plans — instead of inheriting decisions from an earlier life.
Gather common memories. At the end the husband begins, "To think that now we can live wholly for one another —" and Ellida finishes: "And with common memories. Yours, as well as mine."

report: The younger daughter, seeing her father with her stepmother, whispers: "Why, she and father look exactly as if they were a betrothed couple!" After years of marriage they are engaged for real for the first time. In the first act the painter Ballested says he has settled in the town, "united to the place by the bonds of time and habit"; in the last Ellida corrects him: people can settle in — "In freedom they can". The same house, the same fjord, the same husband — but what holds them now is not habit but choice.

unit.title: The bargain nobody named

captions.M: Wanting quiet and a corner where nothing needs explaining
captions.N: Going through unwritten terms that hold you both
captions.D: Choosing each other again — freely and aloud

unit.meaning: Your task is to say your union's unwritten terms aloud and choose each other again, freely and on your own responsibility.
